title: UNIT 1: SEQUENCES AND SERIES
notes:
✓ Sequence → an ordered list of numbers arranged according to a definite rule.

The terms of a sequence are denoted by a₁, a₂, a₃, …, aₙ.

aₙ → the general term or nth term.

◆ Finite sequence → has a finite number of terms.
◆ Infinite sequence → continues without an end.

A sequence can be represented by its terms, a formula for aₙ, a recursive rule, or a graph.

title: 1.1 SEQUENCES
notes:
✓ A sequence is a function whose domain is a set of consecutive integers or natural numbers and whose range consists of the terms of the sequence.

General term → aₙ gives the value of any term when n is known.

To find terms from a formula → substitute n = 1, 2, 3, … into aₙ.

Example: If aₙ = 2n − 1:
a₁ = 1, a₂ = 3, a₃ = 5, a₄ = 7, a₅ = 9.

→ Graph of a sequence consists of isolated points (n, aₙ), because the domain consists of discrete integer values.

title: 1.1.1 RECURSIVE SEQUENCES
notes:
✓ Recursive sequence → a sequence in which one or more terms are defined using terms that come before them.

A recursive definition normally gives:
1. Initial term(s)
2. A rule for obtaining later terms.

Fibonacci sequence → 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, …
Each term after the first two is the sum of the two preceding terms:
Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂.

Mulatu sequence → introduced by Ethiopian mathematician Professor Mulatu Lemma.
M₀ = 4, M₁ = 1, and Mₙ = Mₙ₋₁ + Mₙ₋₂ for n ≥ 2.

Fibonacci and Mulatu sequences are examples of recursively defined sequences.

title: 1.2 ARITHMETIC AND GEOMETRIC SEQUENCES
notes:
✓ Two important types of sequences are arithmetic and geometric sequences.

◆ Arithmetic sequence → consecutive terms have a constant difference.
◆ Geometric sequence → consecutive terms have a constant non-zero ratio.

title: 1.2.1 ARITHMETIC SEQUENCES
notes:
✓ Arithmetic sequence → each term after the first is obtained by adding a fixed number, called the common difference d.

Example: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, …
Common difference: d = 3.

Common difference:
d = aₙ − aₙ₋₁

General term:
aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d

Where:
◆ a₁ → first term
◆ d → common difference
◆ n → position of the term
◆ aₙ → nth term.

title: ARITHMETIC SEQUENCE: IMPORTANT RULES
notes:
✓ If a sequence is arithmetic:

a₂ = a₁ + d
a₃ = a₁ + 2d
a₄ = a₁ + 3d
aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d

Finding d when two terms are known:
aₙ − aₘ = (n − m)d

Therefore:
d = (aₙ − aₘ)/(n − m)

◆ If d > 0 → increasing sequence.
◆ If d < 0 → decreasing sequence.
◆ If d = 0 → constant sequence.

title: ARITHMETIC MEAN
notes:
✓ Arithmetic mean → the number inserted between two numbers to form an arithmetic sequence.

If a, m, b are consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence:
m − a = b − m

Therefore:
m = (a + b)/2

→ To insert several arithmetic means, use the arithmetic-sequence formula and determine the required common difference.

title: 1.2.2 GEOMETRIC SEQUENCES
notes:
✓ Geometric sequence → a sequence in which the ratio between consecutive terms is a non-zero constant.

Common ratio:
r = aₙ/aₙ₋₁

Example: 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, …
r = 2.

General term:
aₙ = a₁rⁿ⁻¹

Where:
◆ a₁ → first term
◆ r → common ratio
◆ n → position
◆ aₙ → nth term.

title: GEOMETRIC SEQUENCE: IMPORTANT RULES
notes:
✓ For a geometric sequence:

a₂ = a₁r
a₃ = a₁r²
a₄ = a₁r³
aₙ = a₁rⁿ⁻¹

If two terms are known:
aₙ/aₘ = rⁿ⁻ᵐ

◆ r > 1 → terms increase in magnitude when the first term is positive.
◆ 0 < r < 1 → terms approach zero when continued indefinitely.
◆ r < 0 → signs alternate between positive and negative.

title: GEOMETRIC MEAN
notes:
✓ Geometric mean → a number inserted between two non-zero numbers so that the resulting terms form a geometric sequence.

If a, m, b are consecutive geometric terms:
m/a = b/m

Therefore:
m² = ab

Geometric mean:
m = √(ab)

→ For appropriate signed values, the sign of m must also satisfy the required common ratio.

title: 1.3 Σ SIGMA NOTATION AND PARTIAL SUMS
notes:
✓ Partial sum → the sum of the first n terms of a sequence.

Sₙ = a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + … + aₙ

✓ Sigma notation → a concise way of writing a long sum using the Greek letter Σ.

General form:
Σₖ₌ₘⁿ aₖ

means:
aₘ + aₘ₊₁ + aₘ₊₂ + … + aₙ.

title: Σ PROPERTIES OF SIGMA NOTATION
notes:
✓ Important properties:

◆ Constant multiple:
Σ(caₖ) = cΣaₖ

◆ Sum of two sequences:
Σ(aₖ + bₖ) = Σaₖ + Σbₖ

◆ Difference:
Σ(aₖ − bₖ) = Σaₖ − Σbₖ

◆ Constant:
Σc = nc, when n terms are being summed.

→ Sigma notation is useful for representing both finite sums and the partial sums used to study infinite series.

title: TELESCOPING SEQUENCES
notes:
✓ Telescoping sequence/series → a sum in which consecutive terms cancel when expanded.

Example structure:
(a₁ − a₂) + (a₂ − a₃) + (a₃ − a₄) + …

→ Most intermediate terms cancel, leaving only the first and last terms.

Telescoping is useful for finding partial sums quickly.

title: 1.3.2 SUM OF ARITHMETIC SEQUENCES
notes:
✓ For an arithmetic sequence with first term a₁, last term aₙ, common difference d, and n terms:

Sum of first n terms:
Sₙ = n/2 [2a₁ + (n − 1)d]

Also:
Sₙ = n/2(a₁ + aₙ)

Sum of the first n natural numbers:
1 + 2 + 3 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2

→ These formulas can be used when the first term, last term, common difference, or number of terms is known.

title: ARITHMETIC SUM PROBLEMS
notes:
To solve an arithmetic-series problem:

1. Identify a₁, d and n, or identify a₁ and aₙ.

2. Find any missing term using:
aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d

3. Use:
Sₙ = n/2(a₁ + aₙ)

→ For a sequence whose terms represent quantities increasing or decreasing by a constant amount, the total is found using the arithmetic-series formula.

title: 1.3.3 SUM OF GEOMETRIC SEQUENCES
notes:
✓ For a geometric sequence with first term a₁, common ratio r, and n terms:

Finite geometric sum:
Sₙ = a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r),  r ≠ 1

Equivalent form:
Sₙ = a₁(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1)

If r = 1:
Sₙ = na₁.

→ Use the formula when the terms form a geometric progression.

title: 1.4 INFINITE SERIES
notes:
✓ Infinite series → the sum of infinitely many terms of a sequence.

An infinite sequence lists terms indefinitely.

An infinite series is formed by adding those terms.

Example:
a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + …

→ The partial sum Sₙ is used to investigate whether the infinite series approaches a finite value.

title: 1.4.1 CONVERGENCE AND DIVERGENCE
notes:
✓ Convergent sequence → approaches a finite limit as n → ∞.

◆ Divergent to +∞ → terms increase without bound.
◆ Divergent to −∞ → terms decrease without bound.
◆ Vibrating/oscillating sequence → does not approach a single limit because its values continue to oscillate.

For a geometric sequence aₙ = a₁rⁿ⁻¹:

◆ |r| < 1 → aₙ → 0, so the sequence converges.
◆ r = 1 → constant sequence.
◆ r > 1 → diverges in magnitude.
◆ r ≤ −1 → generally oscillates/diverges.

title: INFINITE GEOMETRIC SERIES
notes:
✓ For:
a₁ + a₁r + a₁r² + a₁r³ + …

The infinite geometric series converges only when:
|r| < 1

Its sum is:
S∞ = a₁/(1 − r)

If |r| ≥ 1 → the infinite geometric series does not have a finite sum; it diverges or oscillates.

Example:
1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + …

S∞ = 1/(1 − 1/2) = 2.

title: RECURRING DECIMALS AS INFINITE SERIES
notes:
✓ A recurring/repeating decimal can be represented as an infinite geometric series and converted into a fraction.

Example:
0.3333… = 0.3 + 0.03 + 0.003 + …

This is a geometric series with:
a₁ = 0.3 and r = 0.1.

Therefore:
S∞ = 0.3/(1 − 0.1) = 1/3.

→ A repeating decimal can therefore be expressed as a rational number.

title: 1.5 APPLICATIONS OF SEQUENCES AND SERIES IN DAILY LIFE
notes:
✓ Sequences and series are used to model real-life situations involving regular increases, decreases, growth, repeated changes and patterns.

◆ Arithmetic sequences → situations with a constant increase or decrease.

Examples → salaries increasing by a fixed amount, production increasing by a fixed number, regularly spaced quantities.

◆ Geometric sequences → situations involving multiplication by a constant factor.

Examples → percentage growth, depreciation, repeated reduction, compound-type growth, and repeated proportional changes.

→ Choose arithmetic when the change is constant.
→ Choose geometric when the ratio or percentage change is constant.

title: APPLICATION FORMULAS
notes:
For regular fixed increases:
aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d
Sₙ = n/2(a₁ + aₙ)

For repeated proportional growth:
aₙ = a₁rⁿ⁻¹

For a geometric total:
Sₙ = a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)

For an infinite geometric process with |r| < 1:
S∞ = a₁/(1 − r)

→ Word problems should first be translated into a sequence or series before choosing the formula.

title: UNIT 1 KEY TERMS & FORMULAS
notes:
✓ Sequence → ordered list of numbers following a rule.

General term → aₙ, the nth term.

Recursive sequence → terms defined using preceding terms.

Arithmetic sequence → constant difference d.

Arithmetic nth term → aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d.

Arithmetic sum → Sₙ = n/2(a₁ + aₙ).

Geometric sequence → constant ratio r.

Geometric nth term → aₙ = a₁rⁿ⁻¹.

Geometric mean → m = √(ab).

Finite geometric sum → Sₙ = a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r).

Partial sum → sum of the first n terms.

Sigma notation → Σ, compact notation for sums.

Infinite series → sum of infinitely many terms.

Convergent → approaches a finite limit.

Divergent → does not approach a finite limit.

Infinite geometric sum → S∞ = a₁/(1 − r), when |r| < 1.
